messages.subject: Numerous variables and interactions
parts:
Hi all,

I have a lot of variables and I'm not sure how to go about dealing with them...I have considered reducing my dataset via a PCA but previous threads suggest that this is not such a good idea, especially when procD.lm can handle data with high dimensionality.

I averaged my shape data by female so I have 2 observations per female: one for each developmental stage. (NB: developmental stage did not seem to effect shape so to try and reduce model complexity I dropped this variable from the analysis).

I am interested in understanding how shape changes with: 1) population; 2) mean egg size of female; 3) coefficient of variation of egg size per female; 4) mean offspring size once hatched at both developmental stages (meanSize; i.e. my equivalent of Csize); 5) female; and finally 6) mean gene expression per female across 14 genes. 

This is what my model looks like:
procD.lm(shape ~ log(meanSize) * meanEggSize * eggCV * pop + Star.log + Igf1.log + Gr.log + Sgk1.log + Mtor.log + Ghr1.log + Rictor.log + 
                 Igf2.log + Timp2.log + Sparc.log + Ctsk.log + Ets2.log + Mmp2.log + Mmp9.log,
               data = female.gdf.symm, iter = 999, RRPP = T)

I can not include female in here because I get the error "subscript is out of bounds". I can, however, nest female within population (which has the lowest residual SS) but given the high number of variables and interactions, nested.update seems almost impossible. Instead, I decided to remove female since it is likely confounded by meanEggSize per female.

Based on preliminary procD.lm results (sequentially adding variables to the last position to obtain unbiased estimates), 'geneX*pop' often has a significant interaction. The best way I can think of testing how gene expression of each gene varies with shape within populations is to run each gene separately in advanced.procD.lm and obtaining pairwise comparisons. I am also interested in whether gene expression * egg size and egg size variation (eggCV) can have an effect on shape too. To do this I tried:

advanced.procD.lm(f1 = shape ~ log(meanSize) * meanEggSize * eggCV * pop + Star.log + Igf1.log + Gr.log + Sgk1.log + Mtor.log + Ghr1.log + Rictor.log + Igf2.log + Timp2.log + Sparc.log + Ctsk.log + Ets2.log + Mmp2.log + Mmp9.log,
                 f2 = ~ log(meanSize) * meanEggSize * eggCV * pop * Star.log + Igf1.log + Gr.log + Sgk1.log + Mtor.log + Ghr1.log + Rictor.log + 
                   Igf2.log + Timp2.log + Sparc.log + Ctsk.log + Ets2.log + Mmp2.log + Mmp9.log,
                 groups = ~pop, iter = 99,
               data = female.gdf.symm,RRPP = T) 

But receive the error "Error in `[.data.frame`(m, xvars) : undefined columns selected".

To go around this problem, I subsetted my data into populations and tested the same model within populations. But then I run into the problem "Models have same df" despite having an interaction term in f2 but not in f1:
advanced.procD.lm(f1 = shape ~ log(meanSize) * meanEggSize * eggCV + Star.log + Igf1.log + Gr.log + Sgk1.log + Mtor.log + Ghr1.log + Rictor.log + 
                 Igf2.log + Timp2.log + Sparc.log + Ctsk.log + Ets2.log + Mmp2.log + Mmp9.log,
                 f2 = ~ log(meanSize)  * meanEggSize* eggCV * Star.log + Igf1.log + Gr.log + Sgk1.log + Mtor.log + Ghr1.log + Rictor.log + 
                   Igf2.log + Timp2.log + Sparc.log + Ctsk.log + Ets2.log + Mmp2.log + Mmp9.log,
                 groups = ~eggCV, iter = 99,
               data = FJgdf,RRPP = T) 



If anyone has any suggestions on what might be happening here then that would be great! And also whether my method of analysing such data is correct?

Thanks,
Sam

messages.author: e9e8ab1df38d9a77
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Numerous variables and interactions
parts:
Sam

 Just for clarification, when you say you used PCA, did you mean on the response data (shape data here) (which is unnecessary for geomorph) or for the matrix of predictors (i.e. on X(^T)X or something akin to that)? Certainly this could be done on the log transformed gene expression values for the 14 genes (i.e. it may be that much of the gene expression is highly correlated), and use a few PCs of gene expression reducing the number of predictors.

I am not sure how many observations you have (2 per female, but not sure how many females), nor how many landmarks you have, but I am going to suggest that with this many predictors, and no clear hierarchy for them (ie. which should be used for model fitting first) it is possible that a standard model selection procedures may not be entirely effective and likely not particulalry informative. Off the top of my head there are a few potential ways of dealing with this.

1 - First 2 block partial least squares MIGHT be an informative approach to dealing with this. However you will want to standardize your predictors (even qualitative ones) prior to the analysis to help with interpretation (and so that predictors with large values, and likely large (co)variances don't overwhelm).

2 - Have you thought about utilizing some form of regularization/shrinkage? i.e. using a ridge or lasso approach for your problem for instance? That is fit all predictors simultaneously, but enable some form of shrinkage on their estimated coefficients. This can improve stability, and with lasso also interpretability (if some of the terms are shrunk to zero). This can be done with glmnet (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/glmnet/index.html) with the mgaussian family (although you may need to perform a PCA on the shape data first and use the 2p-4 PC if it is 2D data). However, for this approach to be feasible you need to have enough data (i.e. observations) to be able to perform cross-validation.

Good luck!

Ian Dworkin

Samantha,

 

The left and right singular vectors are not for plotting: they are the PLS axes themselves. The scores are what one plots. A careful reading of both the help file, as well as the primary literature, will make things more clear.

 

As to your other question: PLS does not describe overall variation. It describes covariation between the two blocks. The output object has a component $svd.  This, has a component $d, which contains the singular values from the analysis. One can use these to calculate the percent CO-variation described by each set of PLS axes with one another.

Sam,

 

Groups are not incorporated in a PLS analysis: it is not a linear model. Instead, and as I stated previously, 2B-PLS characterizes covariation between two blocks of variables: nothing more.  Note that this holds for the function ‘integration.test’ because performs a PLS.

 

The code you sent using Map simply loops over groups and performs separate analyses on each (assuming head.coords.gp and tail.coords.gp are both set up as lists by group). Thus, the function does precisely what you described earlier: it ran a PLS on each group separately. Note, ‘x’ and ‘y’ here are place-holders for Map to go and grab the components out of the two data lists. When this is done, each analysis is in fact, run the analysis on all shape variables.

 

I suggest digging a bit deeper into both basic R programming and statistical methods. The geomorph team is very happy to assist users in their geomorph analyses, but we cannot use this forum in the place of workshops or courses in morphometric theory, statistical theory, or basic R use. That component of learning still does rest on the scientists who wish to use geomorph to accomplish their morphometric analysis.


Best,

Dean

procD.lm(shape ~ log(meanSize) * meanEggSize * eggCV * pop + Star.log + Igf1.log + Gr.log + Sgk1.log + Mtor.log + Ghr1.log + Rictor.log + 

                 Igf2.log + Timp2.log + Sparc.log + Ctsk.log + Ets2.log + Mmp2.log + Mmp9.log,

               data = female.gdf.symm, iter = 999, RRPP = T)

 

I can not include female in here because I get the error "subscript is out of bounds". I can, however, nest female within population (which has the lowest residual SS) but given the high number of variables and interactions, nested.update seems almost impossible. Instead, I decided to remove female since it is likely confounded by meanEggSize per female.

 

Based on preliminary procD.lm results (sequentially adding variables to the last position to obtain unbiased estimates), 'geneX*pop' often has a significant interaction. The best way I can think of testing how gene expression of each gene varies with shape within populations is to run each gene separately in advanced.procD.lm and obtaining pairwise comparisons. I am also interested in whether gene expression * egg size and egg size variation (eggCV) can have an effect on shape too. To do this I tried:

 

advanced.procD.lm(f1 = shape ~ log(meanSize) * meanEggSize * eggCV * pop + Star.log + Igf1.log + Gr.log + Sgk1.log + Mtor.log + Ghr1.log + Rictor.log + Igf2.log + Timp2.log + Sparc.log + Ctsk.log + Ets2.log + Mmp2.log + Mmp9.log,

                 f2 = ~ log(meanSize) * meanEggSize * eggCV * pop * Star.log + Igf1.log + Gr.log + Sgk1.log + Mtor.log + Ghr1.log + Rictor.log + 

                   Igf2.log + Timp2.log + Sparc.log + Ctsk.log + Ets2.log + Mmp2.log + Mmp9.log,

                 groups = ~pop, iter = 99,

               data = female.gdf.symm,RRPP = T)

advanced.procD.lm(f1 = shape ~ log(meanSize) * meanEggSize * eggCV + Star.log + Igf1.log + Gr.log + Sgk1.log + Mtor.log + Ghr1.log + Rictor.log +
